title: Theo and the Letter
premise: Insurance investigator Oscar Okafor receives a confession letter for a drowning ruled accidental — postmarked the day after the victim's funeral, and addressed to him by name. The letter's details match the case file with impossible precision, including facts never made public, forcing Oscar to admit the writer is either the killer or someone inside the investigation. As he reopens the case in the coastal town of Greywater Bay, a second letter arrives correcting the first, and Oscar realizes the confessor is being fed information — and eliminated as a loose end. The trail leads to a decades-old wrongful conviction that the town's founding families buried, and to the tide itself, which finally gives up what it took: the victim's true identity, hidden in plain sight. In the end, Oscar must choose between handing his evidence to the corrupt local police and letting the town mete out its own justice, and he chooses neither — he publishes everything, giving the dead their names back.
about_author: A. M. Kavanagh is the pen name of a former maritime claims adjuster who spent eleven years investigating deaths at sea before turning to fiction. They write from a house within earshot of a working harbor, where the tide still dictates the day's schedule.

chapters.title: Postmarked Grief
chapters.summary: Oscar Okafor, sorting cold cases after a forced leave, opens a confession letter for drowned fisherman Elias Wren — postmarked the day after the funeral. The letter cites file details only investigators could know. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: unease curdling into obsession as his photographic memory confirms every detail matches.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot on Purpose
chapters.summary: Oscar travels to Greywater Bay under cover of a routine claims review. The town is warm, closed, and rehearsed; everyone loved Elias, no one saw anything. He meets constable Dana Voss, who warns him off with genuine fear rather than hostility. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being an outsider among people protecting something.

chapters.title: Second Letter, First Correction
chapters.summary: A second letter arrives at Oscar's hotel, amending the confession: the writer claims they were coerced, that someone else held the pen. It includes a detail about the tide table that contradicts the official timeline. POV: Oscar, with a brief interlude in the anonymous writer's voice. Emotional beat: dread — the confessor is alive, scared, and reachable.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: Oscar walks the shoreline at low tide and finds the physical evidence the letters predicted: a weighted tarp fragment snagged below the old pier. Before he can secure it, someone burns a shed nearby to destroy the scene. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: the shift from investigator to target; the case wants him gone.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Elias
chapters.summary: Dental records don't match. The man buried as Elias Wren was a stranger — possibly connected to a 1998 wrongful conviction of a dockworker named Samuel Adeyemi, whose family once lived where Oscar's own father grew up. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: personal vertigo; this case has been waiting for him specifically.

chapters.title: Everyone Signed Something
chapters.summary: Oscar discovers the town's founding families all hold shares in a shell company tied to the old conviction — hush money compounding for twenty-five years. Dana Voss quietly passes him a sealed personnel file, choosing a side. POV: alternating Oscar and Dana. Emotional beat: fragile alliance; belonging offered at a price.

chapters.title: The Third Letter Is a Summons
chapters.summary: A third letter sets a meeting at the decommissioned lighthouse, naming the writer: Marion Wren, Elias's widow, who confesses she helped stage the drowning to expose the conspiracy — but the stranger who died wasn't supposed to be there. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: the mystery inverts; the confession was bait all along.

chapters.title: Better Than the File
chapters.summary: At the lighthouse, Oscar realizes the killer is Aldous Crane, the retired lead investigator on the 1998 case, who has been feeding Marion scripted confessions to control the narrative and eliminate witnesses. Crane springs his trap, knowing Oscar's every move because he wrote the playbook Oscar trained on. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: terror and clarity — beat the teacher at his own game.

chapters.title: The Tide Gives Up What It Took
chapters.summary: Oscar turns Crane's file-obsession against him, feeding false details through Dana that lure Crane back to the pier to destroy evidence as the spring tide exposes the original victim's remains and Crane's signature weight rig. Dana arrests him with federal witnesses present. POV: Oscar and Dana. Emotional beat: cathartic reversal; justice arrives on the water's schedule, not Crane's.

chapters.title: Names for the Dead
chapters.summary: Oscar declines to bury the town's complicity with the case file: he publishes the full record, restoring Samuel Adeyemi's name and giving the unidentified victim one too. Marion faces her charges without excuses; Dana rebuilds the constabulary; Oscar stays through one more tide. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: quiet resolution — belonging found not in the town's approval, but in telling the truth it couldn't bear.
